# Introduction

This vignette shows the statistical methods added to ScreenR in version
1.15.4 and explains why they were added. It complements the vignette
*ScreenR Example Analysis*, which shows the complete pipeline.

| Topic | New or changed functions |
|-------|--------------------------|
| Design matrix and contrasts | `create_design_matrix()`, `create_contrast()` |
| Significance of CAMERA and ROAST hits | `fdr` and `seed` arguments, `Log2FC` column |
| Fold change of barcodes with zero reads | `pseudocount` argument of `compute_metrics()` |
| Normalization | `method` argument of `normalize_data()` |
| Gene-level Z-score test | `find_gene_zscore_hit()` |
| Replicate-aware barcode statistics | `compute_barcode_statistics()` |
| One model for the whole time course | `find_time_hit()` |
| Combining the methods | `summarise_hits()` |
| Quality control | `plot_replicate_correlation()`, `compute_gini()`, `find_discordant_barcodes()` |

```{r packages}
library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Data

We use the example dataset of the package: an shRNA chemical lethality screen
with 10 barcodes for most genes, two early time points (Time1 and Time2) and
treated (TRT) and control (CTRL) samples in triplicate at two later time points
(Time3 and Time4).

```{r data}
data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)

counts <- count_table
colnames(counts) <- c(
    "Barcode", "Time1", "Time2", "Time3_TRT_A", "Time3_TRT_B", "Time3_TRT_C",
    "Time3_CTRL_A", "Time3_CTRL_B", "Time3_CTRL_C",
    "Time4_TRT_A", "Time4_TRT_B", "Time4_TRT_C",
    "Time4_CTRL_A", "Time4_CTRL_B", "Time4_CTRL_C"
)
counts <- counts %>%
    mutate(Barcode = as.factor(Barcode)) %>%
    filter(Barcode != "*") %>%
    tibble()

groups <- factor(c(
    "T1/T2", "T1/T2",
    rep("Time3_TRT", 3), rep("Time3_CTRL", 3),
    rep("Time4_TRT", 3), rep("Time4_CTRL", 3)
))

object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups,
    replicates = ""
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
object <- normalize_data(object)
object <- compute_data_table(object)
```

# Quality control

## Replicate correlation

Replicates of the same condition should be more similar to each other than to
the other samples. `plot_replicate_correlation()` shows the correlation of the
log2 counts per million between all the pairs of samples.

```{r replicate-correlation, fig.height = 6}
plot_replicate_correlation(object)
```

## Library evenness

The Gini index measures how unevenly the reads are spread over the barcodes:
0 means all the barcodes have the same number of reads, values close to 1 mean
that a few barcodes take most of the reads. In a dropout screen it usually
increases over time; a strong increase or a large difference between
replicates can signal a bottleneck.

`compute_gini()` returns the values and `plot_gini()` plots them.

```{r gini}
compute_gini(object)
plot_gini(object)
```

## Normalization

By default `normalize_data()` divides by the total number of reads of each
sample (`method = "cpm"`). When strong hits deplete a large part of the
library, the total number of reads is a biased measure of the sequencing
depth. `method = "tmm"` corrects it with the TMM normalization factors of
edgeR, and `method = "control"` normalizes to a set of control barcodes (for
example non-targeting shRNAs), when the library has them.

```{r normalization}
object_tmm <- normalize_data(object, method = "tmm")

# Ratio between the TMM and the total-count normalized values of each sample
ratio <- colMeans(SummarizedExperiment::assay(object_tmm, "normalized")) /
    colMeans(SummarizedExperiment::assay(object, "normalized"))
tibble(Sample = names(ratio), TMM_over_CPM = round(ratio, 3))
```

In this dataset the two methods agree within a few percent, so we keep the
default.

# Design matrix and contrasts

The edgeR/limma based methods need a design matrix and a contrast. A common
pitfall is to rename the columns of `model.matrix(~ groups)`:
`model.matrix()` orders the columns alphabetically by group and the first group
becomes the intercept, so renaming them in another order silently compares the
wrong samples.

```{r design-pitfall}
wrong <- model.matrix(~groups)
colnames(wrong) <- unique(groups)
# The column called "Time3_TRT" actually marks the Time3_CTRL samples
as.character(groups[wrong[, "Time3_TRT"] == 1])
```

`create_design_matrix()` creates a design matrix with one column for each group
(no intercept) and `create_contrast()` creates the comparison between groups by
name, which avoids this problem.

```{r design}
design <- create_design_matrix(object)
colnames(design)

contrasts <- list(
    Time3 = create_contrast(design,
        treatment = "Time3_TRT", control = "Time3_CTRL"
    ),
    Time4 = create_contrast(design,
        treatment = "Time4_TRT", control = "Time4_CTRL"
    )
)
contrasts$Time4
```

# CAMERA and ROAST with a significance cut off

`find_camera_hit()` and `find_roast_hit()` now return only the genes with an
FDR lower or equal to `fdr` (default 0.05) and report `Log2FC`, the median log2
fold change of the barcodes of each gene. Previously CAMERA returned all the
genes with the requested direction (about half of the genes) and ROAST used the
raw p-value.

The p-values are **one-sided** for the requested direction: camera and roast
report two-sided p-values, which are twice too large for a test of depletion
only. The FDR is computed from the one-sided p-values over all the genes, with
the Benjamini-Hochberg method or, with `fdr_method = "storey"`, with the less
conservative Storey method when many genes have an effect.

ROAST uses random rotations: the `seed` argument makes the result
reproducible, and its smallest p-value is 1 / (`nrot` + 1). `method = "fry"`
uses `limma::fry()`, an exact and fast approximation of ROAST with continuous
p-values. ROAST and fry are self-contained tests (does the gene change?),
while CAMERA is competitive (does the gene change more than the others?) and
becomes conservative when many genes have an effect.

```{r camera-roast}
camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrasts$Time4, fdr = 1)
roast <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrasts$Time4,
    nrot = 999, seed = 42, fdr = 1
)
fry <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrasts$Time4,
    method = "fry", fdr = 1
)

# Number of genes at different FDR levels
fdr_levels <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25)
tibble(
    FDR = fdr_levels,
    CAMERA = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(camera$FDR <= x), 1L),
    ROAST = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(roast$FDR <= x), 1L),
    fry = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(fry$FDR <= x), 1L)
)

head(camera)
```

The treatment effect in this example dataset is weak: at Time4 there are
`r sum(camera$FDR <= 0.05)` genes at an FDR of 5% with CAMERA,
`r sum(roast$FDR <= 0.05)` with ROAST and `r sum(fry$FDR <= 0.05)` with fry; at
an FDR of 25% there are `r sum(camera$FDR <= 0.25)`, `r sum(roast$FDR <= 0.25)`
and `r sum(fry$FDR <= 0.25)`.

# A gene-level test for the Z-score

## Why a new test

`find_zscore_hit()` calls a gene a hit when more than `number_barcode` of its
barcodes have a Z-score below the median Z-score. By definition half of all
barcodes are below the median, so for a gene without any effect the number of
such barcodes is binomial with probability 0.5. With 10 barcodes and
`number_barcode = 6` the probability of being called a hit by chance is

```{r null-probability}
pbinom(6, size = 10, prob = 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

so about 17% of the genes without any effect are called hits.

## The test

`find_gene_zscore_hit()` computes for each gene a score, the mean (or, with
`statistic = "median"`, the median) of the Z-scores of its barcodes, and
compares it with the scores of many random sets of barcodes of the same size
(`n_permutations`, default 100000). The p-value is the proportion of random
sets with a score at least as extreme. This permutation test makes no
assumption on the distribution of the Z-scores and gives continuous,
well-calibrated p-values. The random barcodes are drawn from the whole library
or, when the library has them, only from non-targeting controls
(`control_genes`), which is the best reference because it does not contain the
barcodes of the true hits. The p-values are corrected with the
Benjamini-Hochberg (or Storey) method.

The log2 fold changes are now computed with a pseudocount
(`compute_metrics(pseudocount = 0.5)`, in counts per million), so barcodes
with zero reads in the treated samples get a finite fold change instead of
about -23, which would distort the Z-scores of all the other barcodes.

```{r gene-zscore}
metrics <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time4"
)
range(metrics$Log2FC)

gene_zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(metrics, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore)

c(
    old_rule_hits = nrow(find_zscore_hit(metrics, number_barcode = 6)),
    gene_test_FDR_0.25 = sum(gene_zscore$FDR <= 0.25)
)
```

## Replicate-aware barcode statistics

`compute_metrics()` averages the replicates before computing the fold change,
so a barcode that is noisy across replicates counts as much as a consistent
one. `compute_barcode_statistics()` tests each barcode with the edgeR
quasi-likelihood F-test, which uses the variability between replicates, and
reports a signed Z-score that can be used with `find_gene_zscore_hit()`.

```{r barcode-statistics}
barcode_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(
    object, design, contrasts$Time4
)
head(barcode_statistics)

gene_zscore_edger <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics, fdr = 1,
    seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore_edger)
```

```{r volcano}
ggplot(barcode_statistics, aes(x = Log2FC, y = -log10(PValue))) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(
        x = "Barcode log2 fold change (Time4 TRT vs CTRL)",
        y = "-log10 p-value"
    )
```

# One model for the whole time course

Analysing each time point separately answers "is there an effect at Time3?"
and "is there an effect at Time4?". `find_time_hit()` answers "does the effect
of the treatment change over time?" with a single model,
log(abundance) = a + b * time + d * treated + c * time * treated.
The untreated and the treated samples each follow their own line over the time
points (treated as equally spaced); c is the difference between the two
slopes, i.e. how much the treatment effect changes per time point, and is 0
when the effect is constant. The coefficient c is tested for the barcodes of
each gene with CAMERA. The early time points can be added as untreated
baseline samples, so that the untreated line is estimated from four time
points.

```{r time-model}
time_hit <- find_time_hit(object,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    baseline = c("Time1", "Time2"),
    days = c("Time1", "Time2", "Time3", "Time4"),
    fdr = 1
)
head(time_hit)
```

The column `Log2FC` is the median over the barcodes of the gene of c, the
change of the treatment log2 fold change per time point. The top genes can be
inspected with `plot_trend()`.

```{r time-trend, fig.height = 4}
plot_trend(object,
    genes = time_hit$Gene[1:2], group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "TRT"),
    nrow = 1, ncol = 2
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

# Combining the methods

The overlap between the hits of the three methods can be shown with
`plot_common_hit()`. Here each list contains the genes with an FDR of at most
25% (for the Z-score, the replicate-aware gene-level test).

```{r venn, fig.height = 5}
alpha <- 0.25
plot_common_hit(
    hit_zscore = filter(gene_zscore_edger, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_camera = filter(camera, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_roast = filter(roast, FDR <= alpha),
    show_elements = FALSE, show_percentage = FALSE
)
```

`find_common_hit()` returns the genes in the intersection. `summarise_hits()`
also shows how strongly each gene is supported: it puts the FDR of each method
in one table and adds `MaxFDR`, the largest of them, which can be used as a
conservative score to rank the genes supported by all the methods. Since an
FDR is never smaller than the corresponding p-value, `MaxFDR <= alpha` means
that the gene has a p-value of at most `alpha` in every method: for each single
gene this is a level-`alpha` test, whatever the dependence between the methods.
The list of genes with `MaxFDR <= alpha` does not, however, have a guaranteed
false discovery rate, because the false discoveries of the single methods can
concentrate in their intersection: treat it as a short list to validate.

```{r summary}
summary <- summarise_hits(
    list(
        zscore = gene_zscore_edger, camera = camera,
        roast = roast, time = time_hit
    ),
    fdr = alpha
)
head(summary, 10)
```

In this dataset the genes with `MaxFDR <= 0.25` are:
`r if (any(summary$Hit)) paste(summary$Gene[summary$Hit], collapse = ", ") else "none"`.
The top gene of the time course model is `r time_hit$Gene[1]`.

# Discordant barcodes

A gene can be called a hit because of one or two barcodes with a strong
effect, for example because of off-target effects. `find_discordant_barcodes()`
reports the barcodes whose log2 fold change is more than `threshold` median
absolute deviations away from the median of their gene.

```{r discordant}
discordant <- find_discordant_barcodes(metrics, threshold = 3)
nrow(discordant)
head(discordant)

# Discordant barcodes among the top genes
filter(discordant, Gene %in% head(summary$Gene, 10))
```
